title: Which Staffing or Routing Change Meets Support Targets Under Uncertain Workload?
tagline: ServiceFlow: a support queue reconstructed from its event log. FIFO within priority, waits measured from the original arrival, breaks deducted from staffed time, SLA compliance with open overdue tickets counted separately and P90 always beside the mean, and a seeded queue simulator that reproduces the known answer (three tickets at minute 0 served for 10 minutes each wait 0, 10 and 20, mean 10, last completion at 30) before any random arrival is drawn. Synthetic data; project 04 of the Business Data Lab.
tech: PostgreSQL 16 (append-only ticket events, agent intervals under row locks)
FastAPI 0.162 (commands with idempotency keys, 401/403/409/422 contracts, 501 for the unbuilt)
SQL reference recomputation of every metric over three windows
GitHub Actions (postgres:16 service, hosted runners only)
333 Python tests, 296 TypeScript golden checks, 65 browser tests
note: Everything is synthetic: the three queues, 18 agents, 3,826 tickets and every figure come from a seeded generator whose designed relationships (a long technical P1 tail, a Monday-morning capacity bind, faster resolution above proficiency 4, a +20% holdout) and nine injected defects are published in an injection manifest. The public site is a static demo over a published snapshot; the simulator runs in the browser with the published seed and is labelled an estimate, never a realised staffing benefit. The transactional behaviour (loading events, pausing and resuming work, recording transfers, running and comparing simulations) is verified separately on GitHub-hosted runners against a transient PostgreSQL. Built from a written specification by a coordinating session delegating bounded work to implementation subagents; not a measurement of any real support team.
problem:
The weekly service review argues about one number. Average wait looks fine while a tenth of the technical P1 tickets sit for ten hours; a transfer quietly restarts the clock; a bot acknowledgement counts as a first response; an agent on a break is counted as available; and the staffing proposal is a simulation whose warm-up was left in the average. Nobody can say whether adding one agent on Monday morning would have met the target, because the estimate and the history are measured differently.

ServiceFlow fixes the measurement first: one event log with FIFO within priority, waits and resolution from the original arrival, breaks deducted from staffed time, the utilisation and the waiting tail shown as two numbers, arrival distributions estimated from the training weeks only and validated on the holdout, and simulation estimates kept visibly apart from anything realised.
built:
Two implementations of one contract, checked against a hand calculation and each other.

  • The contract: an append-only ticket event log (created, bot and human replies, assignment, pause and resume, transfer, reopen, abandonment, resolution) replayed into one state per ticket; FIFO within priority; wait, first response and resolution measured from the original arrival, never from a transfer; handling clipped to the window; breaks deducted from staffed time; SLA clocks on the wall-clock calendar with open overdue tickets counted separately; a queue simulator with exponential service, a declared warm-up and a horizon, run on common random numbers so that policies are compared on the same demand path; estimates labelled as estimates.
  • A known-answer fixture written first: one agent, three tickets at minute 0, 10-minute service, so starts at 0, 10 and 20, waits of 0, 10 and 20, a mean wait of 10.0000 and the last completion at 30.0000, plus a rejected-record variant and an empty-population variant. A standard-library script reproduces all 130 figures and counts from the records and checks the 7 fixture hashes.
  • The Python domain, PostgreSQL schema and FastAPI commands: load an event batch with duplicates and out-of-order arrivals handled and every rejection kept with its reason; assign, pause, resume, transfer and resolve under row locks in a fixed order with deadlocks retried then refused; compute every metric over any window and grouping; run a seeded simulation and compare two policies with a paired interval. 333 tests run against PostgreSQL 16 on a GitHub-hosted runner, and an independent SQL recomputation agrees with the domain on all 28 metrics over the full, training and holdout windows.
  • The static site: the same contract in TypeScript with integer seconds and exact rationals, including the seeded generator reimplemented so that the browser reproduces the Python simulator event for event; a queue timeline, a shift grid across a daylight-saving weekend, an SLA review, a simulation studio and an evidence page that runs the golden checks live; 296 golden checks and 65 Playwright tests at four widths and 200% zoom.
  • A deterministic synthetic world: three queues, 18 agents in Berlin and Santiago with shifts declared in local time, 3,826 tickets over twelve weeks with Poisson arrivals by hour of week, a +20% holdout, and nine injected defects (a bot acknowledgement labelled human, a reopen recorded as a new customer, an unqualified assignment, two simultaneous services for one agent, a break counted as available, a transfer that resets the arrival, a warm-up left in a simulation, a shift across the clock change, survey non-response skew) published in a manifest with how each must be handled.

steps.title: The known answer before any randomness
steps.body: One agent, three tickets arriving at minute 0, deterministic 10-minute service. FIFO gives starts at 0, 10 and 20, waits of 0, 10 and 20, a mean wait of 10 minutes and the last completion at minute 30. A standard-library script reproduces the figures from the records and the simulator must return exactly these events before it is allowed a seed.

steps.title: Utilisation and the tail are two numbers
steps.body: Occupancy says how busy the agents were; it says nothing about the tenth of tickets that waited longest. Every screen that shows a mean shows the P90 beside it, and the SLA review counts tickets that are still open and already overdue separately from the compliance rate of the resolved ones.

steps.title: Train on eight weeks, validate on four
steps.body: Arrival intensities by hour of week are estimated from weeks 1 to 8 only. Weeks 9 to 12 carry a designed +20% load that the generator discloses; the simulator's forecast is compared against them rather than against the weeks it learned from.

steps.title: Two modes, disclosed
steps.body: Mode A is the backend on a GitHub-hosted runner with a transient PostgreSQL. Mode B is the public site over a published snapshot; the simulation studio runs in the browser with the published seed and says that nothing is staffed or routed by it.

results:
The shift grid on the synthetic snapshot (Saturday 2026-09-05 UTC, the Santiago clock-change night: four agents on shift, 1,140 staffed minutes after breaks, occupancy 0.31; the night crew's recorded 480-minute shift against the real 420 is the injected defect INJ-08, outlined):

The SLA review on a phone:

What the data supports. Over the twelve weeks the queues took 3,817 accepted tickets (9 more were rejected with their dependants, 70 records in all, every one named in the injection manifest) and completed 3,608. Mean wait to first service is 25.5 minutes (the 291 waits after a transfer are measured separately, not added), mean first response 28.0 minutes with a P90 of 44.2, mean resolution 164.6 minutes; first-response compliance is 95.0% overall but 82.4% for P1 (187 of the 227 P1 tickets that received a human reply were answered within 15 minutes; 9 more P1 tickets were abandoned before any reply and are outside that denominator), resolution compliance 97.8% measured from the original arrival (so a reopened ticket is charged the time it lay closed; 54 of the 79 misses are reopens), no ticket open and overdue at the cutoff; agent occupancy is 0.42 over 447,450 staffed minutes; 11.8% of chat and phone tickets were abandoned (201 before any service, 8 after a transfer while mid-service); surveys were invited on 59.5% of completions, answered by 34.9%, with a CSAT of 0.864 among those who answered. The simulation studio reproduces the known answer in the browser and then re-runs the three published scenarios on the published seed: the baseline (five agents, 3.12 arrivals an hour) has a mean wait of 14.6 minutes and a P90 of 31.0; one more agent brings them to 3.9 and 18.7; the holdout intensity on five agents pushes them to 33.6 and 80.9. Each of these is a single seeded replication of about 30 tickets, so the point estimates are wide (over 200 replications the baseline averages 14.0 with a per-run standard deviation of about 24 minutes); the baseline and the plus-one scenario share one demand path, the holdout scenario does not by design; and the model treats the five technical agents as dedicated servers although three of them also handle billing and onboarding. Replication means with intervals and the paired comparison are being added to the page. These are estimates from a seeded model and the page says so; they are not realised staffing benefits. The generator's designed relationships (a long technical P1 tail, the Monday-morning bind, faster handling above proficiency 4, the +20% holdout) are published in its manifest; nothing here is a finding about any real support team.

Found by review, being fixed. An independent reviewer, briefed to disprove the page, confirmed that the SQL reference reports the whole window as staffed time when no shift overlaps it (the three published windows are unaffected); that a ticket rejected for overlapping another agent interval stays rejected after the ticket it clashed with is itself rejected; that an agent can resume work off shift or inside a recorded break, and that the loader does not enforce shift availability; that an analyst can change an existing ticket's state through the event loader; that the request's dataset version is accepted but never checked; and that an earlier version of this page claimed the SupplyScope reference count (184) for this project's script (137 checks; corrected above). The +20% holdout is a chosen realisation of a seeded series (attempt 7; the first seven ranged from +12.7 to +30.5%), which the generator notes disclose but the site did not. The fixes, the disclosures and their regression tests are the next commits on the branch.

Not built yet: the shift-scenario builder (C07) and the recommendation export (C10) return 501; the queue, compare and survey screens are stubs that say so.
